newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - State Street boosts margin.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - State Street boosts margin.

text.p: State Street Boston Corp's operating leverage in 1996 was a positive 0.2 percent as gains in revenue outstripped higher costs, Chief Financial Officer Ronald O'Kelley said in a telephone interview Wednesday.
Operating leverage was a negative 0.3 percent in 1995, he added. He said the improvement boosted pretax profit as a percentage of revenue to 25.7 percent in 1996 from 25.5 percent in 1995.
"We feel comfortable with that level of operating margin," he said, adding that it is likely to remain in a range of 25 to 26 percent.

"We're a revenue-driven company, and we expect costs will increase as revenue increases," he said. He added that the ratios were more meaningful for a 12-month period instead of looking at any three-month period in isolation.

Earlier Wednesday, State Street said fourth-quarter net income rose 20 percent to $78 million versus a year ago. Earnings per share fully diluted rose 22 percent to $0.95 per share. Fourth-quarter revenue jumped 20 percent from a year ago to $501 million. Operating expenses for the fourth quarter rose 21 percent to $375 million, reflecting the need to support business growth.
For the year, revenue rose 19 percent to $1.9 billion and net income rose 19 percent to $293 million.
O'Kelley declined to comment on Bank of New York Co Inc's recent announcement that it had accumulated a 4.99 percent stake in State Street and wanted to double it.

But O'Kelley said that when using industry benchmarks, State Street preferred to compare itself to service companies such as Automatic Data Processing Inc, Electronic Data Systems Corp and First Data Corp.

In contrast with most banks, he said, State Street derives the loin's share of its revenue from fees. The company is still involved in the commercial banking business, but the main thrust is in providing specialized services to institutional investors.

O'Kelley said the company is aiming to provide more and more capabilities that meet the needs of its customers. He said the biggest 1,000 customers use an average of more than five products each, double the number in 1994.

The CFO said State Street's growth has been driven by the need to remain competitive, as well as by the rapid growth of the company's customers. He said the growth requires spending about $150 million to $160 million a year on expansion projects such as updated software.

Asked how State Street Boston would fare if robust global markets began to contract, O'Kelley said if equity markets worldwide declined 10 percent, State Street revenue would decline only by about one percent. A similar 10 percent decline in bond markets would hurt revenue by less than one percent.
"We're not tied to indices and performance of the markets so much as transactions and flows," he said. He said as money came out of one market it would find its way into another market.

Asked about State Street's dividend policy, O'Kelley said the payout was generally about 20 percent of the after-tax earnings per share. Recent practice has been to raise the dividend every other quarter.

On share buybacks, he said that through the end of 1996, about 3.1 million shares were repurchased out of a 6.0 million share program authorized by the board. The program is designed to offset dilution that would be caused by issuing shares for compensation programs and for acquisitions.
An average of 82 million fully diluted shares were outstanding in the fourth quarter of 1996.
